types.note: Waterbody types. Each merged waterbody gets the first type whose 'when' is true, in the order listed. Expressions use the type fields (variables.json type_fields): area_ha, wb_type, on_drainage, stream_order, n_mws, has_drainage_fields, catchment_ratio, and the fields in 'derived', evaluated first. inflow and ownership are unknown from data and are set only by community answers (questions.json type_questions), so without answers the types are exactly those from data.

types.label: Cannot be typed (old layer)
types.description: The layer lacks drainage, stream order and type fields (WB-10).

types.label: Reservoir (out of scope)
types.description: Very large waterbodies, or ones spanning three or more MWS: dam reservoirs and similar. Outside the scope of village-level analysis.
types.why: The 50 ha cut-off and the three-MWS rule are expert judgement: such waterbodies are managed by irrigation departments rather than villages.

types.label: Large river (out of scope)
types.description: Long or wide river stretches spanning three or more MWS or 50 ha. Outside the scope of village-level analysis.

types.label: River reach
types.description: A wet stretch of a river. Its water depends on upstream flow rather than local storage.

types.label: Canal-fed waterbody
types.description: A waterbody on or fed by a canal. Its water depends on canal releases.

types.label: On-stream tank
types.description: A tank of 1 ha or more on a stream of order 3 or higher, often part of a cascade. Typically irrigation storage. On-stream means on a mapped drainage line, or, from 0.5 ha, with a catchment 20 or more times the waterbody's area.
types.why: Stream order 3 or more and 1 ha or more separates system tanks fed by a stream from small check-dam ponds; expert judgement checked against the census tank class.

types.label: Small on-stream pond
types.description: A pond under 1 ha on a stream of order 3 or higher. On-stream means on a mapped drainage line, or, from 0.5 ha, with a catchment 20 or more times the waterbody's area.

types.label: Headwater pond / check dam
types.description: On a first- or second-order stream: runoff harvesting and recharge structures. On-stream means on a mapped drainage line, or, from 0.5 ha, with a catchment 20 or more times the waterbody's area.

types.label: Village pond
types.description: Off the drainage network, 0.5 ha or more: community ponds fed by local runoff.
types.why: 0.5 ha separates community ponds from farm ponds, which are mostly smaller than 0.5 ha; expert judgement. A community answer on ownership overrides the size rule.

types.label: Farm pond
types.description: Off the drainage network and under 0.5 ha: individual or small group ponds.
types.why: Small ponds off the drainage network are taken as farm ponds; the census records most such ponds as privately owned.

derived.note: On a mapped drainage line, or, for waterbodies of 0.5 ha or more, a catchment 20 or more times its area, which catches channel-fed tanks off the mapped drainage line (added 22 Nov 2026 after the census comparison).

derived.expr: (on_stream or inflow == 'stream') and inflow != 'runoff' and inflow != 'canal'
derived.note: Fed by a stream or nala: on_stream from the data, unless a community answer says its water comes from field runoff or a canal; or a stream according to the answer.

signals.note: Signals of a waterbody. Threshold signals grade 0 below the threshold, 0.5 at it and 1 at the severe value, as in the watershed atlas. Boolean signals ('expr') are 1 when true. Variables are computed in seft/wb/indicators.py; MWS fields come from the home MWS (mws_*, ctx_*, share_*). k, kr and krz are percentages of the waterbody's full extent holding water in kharif, kharif and rabi, and kharif, rabi and zaid.

signals.label: Fills poorly in kharif
signals.note: Kharif fill in years without drought in the home MWS (all years if none) in the lowest 20% (severe 10%) of waterbodies of the same type that hold water in 3 or more years. Pooled because a waterbody's extent counts every year's water, so typical fill differs by type.

signals.label: Loses most water by rabi
signals.note: Water area in rabi at or below 60% of the kharif area (severe 30%).

signals.label: Dries up by summer
signals.note: Water area through zaid (summer) at or below 30% of the kharif area (severe 10%).

signals.label: Filling less than its neighbours, year on year
signals.note: Theil-Sen trend of relative fill (kharif fill divided by the median fill of the tehsil's waterbodies that year) at or below -0.08 a year (severe -0.16): over 2017-24 the waterbody fills about half as well, relative to its neighbours, as it did at first. Dividing by the tehsil's median removes the effect of the year's rainfall (2023 was a drought year almost everywhere).

signals.label: Stopped holding water recently
signals.note: Relative fill (kharif fill divided by the tehsil's median that year) in the last two years at or below 30% (severe 10%) of the first three years, for waterbodies that filled to 30% or more at first. Each of the last two years must also be at 15% fill or less (changed 22 Nov 2026 from their average).

signals.label: Fails in drought years
signals.note: Kharif fill in the home MWS's drought years (4 or more moderate or severe drought weeks) at or below half (severe a quarter) of the fill in other years.

signals.label: No water in summer
signals.note: Mean share of the extent holding water through zaid at or below 5% (severe 1%).

signals.label: Water lasts into rabi
signals.note: Mean share of the extent holding water through rabi at or above 40% (severe 60%).

signals.label: Little second-season cropping around it
signals.note: Mean cropping intensity in the zone of influence at or below 1.2 (severe 1.05).

signals.label: Cropping intensity falling around it
signals.note: Theil-Sen trend of cropping intensity in the zone of influence at or below -0.02 a year (severe -0.05).

signals.label: Summer water falling
signals.note: Theil-Sen trend of the zaid water share at or below -2 percentage points a year (severe -5).

signals.label: Small catchment for its size
signals.note: Catchment no more than 5 times the waterbody's area: it may not produce enough runoff to fill it.

signals.label: Large catchment for its size
signals.note: Catchment 20 or more times the waterbody's area: runoff should be ample, so poor filling points to blocked or diverted inflow.

signals.label: Hard rock aquifer
signals.note: Home MWS on a hard-rock aquifer (watershed context): little storage underground, so surface storage and recharge matter more.

signals.label: Alluvial aquifer
signals.note: Home MWS on an alluvial aquifer (watershed context).

signals.label: Semi-arid or dry sub-humid
signals.note: Home MWS semi-arid or dry sub-humid (watershed rainfall context, from the district normal).

signals.label: Eroding catchment
signals.note: Home MWS with 30% or more sloping land, a runoff ratio of 25% or more, or 4% or more farmland degradation: silt load is likely to be high.

signals.label: Groundwater stressed
signals.note: Block stage of groundwater extraction 70% or more (CGWB semi-critical or worse).

signals.label: Zone of influence known
signals.note: A zone of influence was joined to the waterbody, so the cropping it supports is known.

signals.label: Holds water in 3 or more years and not new
signals.note: Holds water in 3 or more of the 8 years and is not new; most rules need this series length.

signals.grading: A threshold signal is graded 0 when its threshold is not crossed, 0.5 at the threshold, rising in proportion to 1 at the severe threshold (seft/signals.py grade). A yes/no signal is 1 or 0. Pooled signals take their thresholds from percentiles of waterbodies of the same type ('pool'). A signal with a 'gate' is 0 where the gate does not hold.

roles.note: Roles: what a waterbody's water is likely used for, from its landscape. Each is a weight from 0 to 1. A rule's intensity is scaled by the roles it harms, so the same problem counts more where the water matters more. Missing values count as 0 (nz).

roles.label: Irrigation
roles.note: Double and triple cropping in the zone of influence (from 30% of its cropland, full at 80%; 60% of the weight), irrigated share in the home MWS (from 20%, full at 80%), villages naming surface water or canals as their main irrigation source; canal-fed waterbodies get 0.3 more.

roles.label: Kharif drought protection
roles.note: Rainfed farming in the home MWS (full at 40% of the area), weighted by climate: semi-arid 1, dry sub-humid 0.8, humid 0.5.

roles.label: Fishery
roles.note: Share of the home MWS's village area reporting fish community ponds or fish farming in Mission Antyodaya (full at 50%).

roles.label: Livestock water
roles.note: Pastoral land of 5% or more in the home MWS (full at 15%), raised by village livestock density. Mixed crop-livestock MWS without pastoral land do not count, as in the watershed atlas.

roles.label: Recharge and domestic water
roles.expr: clip(0.4 * ifelse(ctx_aquifer == 'hard_rock', 1, 0) * ramp(nz(mws_soge_stage), 50, 100) + 0.3 * ramp(nz(mws_soge_stage), 50, 100) + 0.3 * (1 - min(1, nz(mws_piped_water_coverage))), 0, 1)
roles.note: Groundwater stage of extraction (from 50%, full at 100%), counted twice over on hard rock, and households without piped water.

rules.note: Stress and opportunity rules for waterbodies. 'applies_to' lists the waterbody types a rule is checked for; 'gate' is an extra condition (for example a known zone of influence). Triggers use signal grades (true when above 0). Intensity runs from 0 to 100 and is scaled by the roles named in 'roles' (the highest of them), so a problem counts more where the water matters more. Rule questions are in questions.json (stress_questions, listed by rule). Rules are checked only for waterbodies that hold water in 3 or more of the 8 years and are not new (ctx_regular), except where noted.

rules.label: Inflow shortfall
rules.intensity: 100 * s_poor_fill * (0.5 + 0.5 * max(role_irrigation, role_drought_protection, role_fishery, role_livestock, role_recharge_domestic))
rules.rationale: The waterbody fills to a small part of its extent even in years without drought. A large catchment for its size (ctx_large_catchment) points to blocked inlet channels or diverted runoff; a small catchment (ctx_small_catchment) points to a waterbody too large for its catchment, where inlet works will not help. Silt that built up before 2017 also shows as poor filling rather than a falling trend, more likely where the catchment is eroding (ctx_eroding_catchment): in the census comparison, waterbodies whose present storage is below 80% of the original fill poorly nearly twice as often.
rules.public_note: This waterbody fills only partly in the monsoon, even in normal years (s_poor_fill). If its catchment is large for its size (ctx_large_catchment), inlet channels may be blocked or runoff diverted; if small (ctx_small_catchment), the catchment may not produce enough runoff. Where the catchment is eroding (ctx_eroding_catchment), silt that has built up over the years may also have reduced its storage. Ask whether the inlet channels need clearing and how deep the silt is.
interventions: Clear and repair inlet channels
Desilting where storage has been lost to silt
Catchment treatment where runoff is diverted or the catchment is eroding

rules.label: Poor retention
rules.rationale: Most of the water is gone by rabi. (Drying by summer is common in small waterbodies and is checked only where livestock depend on it.) On alluvium (ctx_alluvium) seepage is a likely cause; on hard rock (ctx_hard_rock) heavy drawdown for irrigation or leakage through the bund or sluice is more likely. Matters most where the water is needed in rabi or summer.
rules.public_note: This waterbody loses most of its water by rabi (s_dries_by_rabi). On alluvial soils (ctx_alluvium) this may be seepage; on hard rock (ctx_hard_rock) it may be heavy drawing for irrigation, or leaks through the bund or a damaged sluice gate. Ask whether the sluice gate holds water.
interventions: Repair sluice gates and bund
Rules for sharing and timing water draws

rules.label: Shrinking or silting
rules.intensity: 100 * s_shrinking * (0.7 + 0.3 * ctx_eroding_catchment) * (0.5 + 0.5 * max(role_irrigation, role_drought_protection, role_fishery, role_livestock, role_recharge_domestic))
rules.rationale: Relative to the tehsil's other waterbodies in the same years, kharif fill has fallen steadily over 2017-24. Siltation is the commonest cause, more likely where the catchment is sloping, has high runoff or degrading land (ctx_eroding_catchment). Encroachment of the bed is another: in the census comparison the rule fires for 32% of waterbodies recorded as encroached against 20% of others. Community questions can separate the two.
rules.public_note: The share of this waterbody that fills in the monsoon has been falling year after year (s_shrinking). Silt from the catchment, or farming and building on the bed, are common reasons, more so where the catchment is sloping or eroding (ctx_eroding_catchment). Desilting and removing encroachment may restore storage; ask how deep the silt is and whether the bed is being cultivated.
interventions: Desilting
Catchment treatment against erosion
Remove encroachment of the bed

rules.label: Stopped holding water
rules.intensity: 100 * s_sudden_loss * (0.5 + 0.5 * max(role_irrigation, role_drought_protection, role_fishery, role_livestock, role_recharge_domestic))
rules.rationale: The waterbody filled well in 2017-19 but hardly at all in the last two years. A breached bund, a blocked or diverted inlet, deliberate draining or encroachment are likely; this needs a field check rather than a remote diagnosis. Since 22 Nov 2026 only for waterbodies of 0.25 ha or more, and only where each of the last two years filled to 15% or less: small ponds vary too much from year to year. With these limits the rule fires 2.5 times as often where the census records the waterbody as under repair.
rules.public_note: This waterbody used to fill well but has held little or no water in the last two years (s_sudden_loss). The bund may have breached, the inlet may be blocked, or the bed may have been drained or taken over. Ask what changed.
interventions: Bund or breach repair
Clear the inlet
Remove encroachment

rules.label: Fails in drought years
rules.rationale: Kharif fill falls to half or less in the home MWS's drought years, where rainfed farming depends on it for protective irrigation. Deepening, catchment improvements or linking to a larger source raise drought resilience.
rules.public_note: In drought years this waterbody fills to half or less of its usual level (s_drought_failure), just when rainfed crops nearby need protective irrigation. Ask how crops fared in recent drought years and whether the water was shared fairly.
interventions: Deepening and desilting for more carry-over storage
Water sharing rules for protective irrigation in dry spells

rules.label: Water not reaching fields
rules.rationale: Water lasts into rabi, but cropping intensity in the zone of influence is low or falling. Distribution channels, fair-sharing arrangements or the absence of a water user group may be limiting use; this is a management opportunity rather than a water shortage. In the census comparison the rule fires for 18% of waterbodies with a water user association against 39% of those without one.
rules.public_note: This waterbody holds water into rabi (s_water_lasts), but fields around it grow little in the second season (s_zoi_low_ci) or less than before (s_zoi_ci_decline). Field channels, sharing rules or a water user association, which most waterbodies here lack, could help farmers use the water.
interventions: Repair field channels and outlets
Form or revive a water user association with sharing rules

rules.label: No summer water for livestock
rules.rationale: In a pastoral setting, the waterbody holds no water in summer, when animals depend most on surface water.
rules.public_note: Livestock graze in this area, but this waterbody holds no water in summer (s_no_summer_water). Deepening part of it, or a separate cattle trough fed from it, could keep drinking water for animals.
interventions: Deepen a section for dry-season storage
Cattle troughs

rules.label: Fishery candidate
rules.rationale: Villages around it practise fishery, and the waterbody holds water into rabi, long enough for a fish crop. A candidate for discussion rather than a finding: since 22 Nov 2026 it needs a fishery role of 0.5 or more, because in the census comparison how long water lasts did not separate waterbodies used for pisciculture from others, while the fishery role did.
rules.public_note: Villages here fish in community ponds (role: fishery), and this waterbody holds water into rabi (s_water_lasts). It may support fish rearing by a group, under the panchayat's lease rules.
interventions: Fish seed stocking by a group or cooperative
Panchayat fishing lease

rules.label: Too short-lived for fishery
rules.rationale: Villages around it practise fishery, but the waterbody loses most of its water by rabi, too early for a fish crop.
rules.public_note: Villages here fish in community ponds, but this waterbody loses most of its water by rabi (s_dries_by_rabi), too early for a fish crop. Better retention would help.
interventions: Improve retention (sluice and bund repair, deepening)

rules.label: Short of canal water
rules.rationale: A canal-fed waterbody that fills poorly or loses water by rabi may be at the tail end of the canal, or getting irregular releases.
rules.public_note: This waterbody is fed by a canal but fills poorly or dries by rabi (s_poor_fill, s_dries_by_rabi). It may be at the tail of the canal or receive irregular releases. Ask when canal water arrives here.
interventions: Rotation schedule agreed with the irrigation department
Water user association at the outlet

rules.label: River drying in summer
rules.intensity: 100 * max(s_dry_season_decline, min(s_no_summer_water, s_shrinking)) * (0.5 + 0.5 * max(role_irrigation, role_livestock, role_recharge_domestic))
rules.rationale: The river stretch holds less water in summer over the years. Upstream extraction or falling groundwater (ctx_gw_stressed) reducing baseflow are likely causes; sand mining is another, not visible in the data.
rules.public_note: This stretch of river holds less water in summer than it used to (s_dry_season_decline). Pumping upstream or falling groundwater may be reducing its flow. Ask whether sand is being mined here.
interventions: Regulate pumping from the river in summer
Recharge in the catchment

confidence_scale.high: the data measure the problem directly and the rule has been checked against field records
confidence_scale.medium: the data point to the problem through a close proxy, and the census check supports the direction
confidence_scale.low: the data give an indirect sign; community answers should decide

evaluation: The rule applies only to the waterbody types in applies_to.
Its gate must hold (for example, the waterbody holds water regularly, or its zone of influence is known); otherwise it is not applicable.
Signals are graded from the waterbody's variables and its home MWS; roles are computed from the same.
The trigger combines signal grades (a grade above 0 counts as true) and roles. If it is false and a signal it names has no value, the result is insufficient data.

If triggered, intensity (0-100) is computed from the grades and scaled by the roles the rule names: a problem counts more where the water matters more. A triggered rule is severe at severe_at or more.
Community answers then turn the result into a probability (questions.json assessment).

schemes._about: Government schemes that can fund the interventions named by the waterbody rules (rules.json), and the farm-pond schemes behind the 'recent ponds' count. Each scheme keeps the id it has in knowledge/schemes.json (the watershed atlas) where it exists there. 'states' limits a scheme to waterbodies in those states (null = all states). Each link says which of the rule's interventions the scheme can fund; 'types' optionally limits a link to some waterbody types. Status notes were checked on the date in 'verified' and should be checked again before use: scheme names, periods and guidelines change.

schemes.name: Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-G RAM G)
components: desilting and bund repair (as wage works)
schemes.status: In force since 1 July 2026; replaces MGNREGS
schemes.status_note: The VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 came into force on 1 July 2026 and repealed the Mahatma Gandhi NREGA, 2005. It guarantees 125 days of wage work (up from 100). Its 'water security' priority area covers water conservation structures, irrigation support, groundwater recharge and rejuvenation of water bodies. Whether desilting and farm ponds are listed by name in the new schedules was not confirmed; check the state's works list. Works are planned through the gram panchayat.

schemes.name: Mission Amrit Sarovar (Phase II)
schemes.department: Ministry of Rural Development (with Jal Shakti and other ministries)
components: new ponds of 1 acre or more
user groups that maintain the pond and remove silt after each monsoon
fishery and other uses by user groups
schemes.status_note: More than 68,000 Amrit Sarovars were completed by March 2025 against a target of 50,000. Phase II continues with a focus on water availability and community participation. It has no budget of its own: works are funded through VB-G RAM G (earlier MGNREGS), 15th Finance Commission grants, the PMKSY watershed component, CSR and crowdfunding. User groups, mostly from SHGs, maintain the ponds and remove silt after each monsoon.

schemes.name: Repair, Renovation and Restoration (RRR) of water bodies, under PMKSY - Har Khet Ko Pani
schemes.department: Ministry of Jal Shakti (with the state water resources / minor irrigation department)
schemes.status: Approved for 2021-26; check whether extended beyond March 2026
schemes.status_note: RRR is a component of PMKSY-HKKP, which was approved for 2021-26. Guidelines (2022) target water bodies with a culturable command area of about 40 ha and above (smaller in hilly and special-category areas), proposed by the state. Small farm ponds and village ponds are generally below its size range; it fits onstream tanks and larger canal-fed tanks.

schemes.name: PMKSY - Command Area Development and Water Management (CAD&WM)
schemes.status: Approved for 2021-26; check whether extended beyond March 2026
schemes.status_note: Part of PMKSY-HKKP. Fits canal-fed waterbodies and the commands of larger tanks, where the problem is water distribution rather than storage.

schemes.name: PMKSY - Per Drop More Crop (micro-irrigation)
schemes.department: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
schemes.status_note: Helps farmers use stored pond water efficiently, which matters where a pond holds water but little rabi crop is grown around it.

schemes.name: PMKSY - Watershed Development Component (WDC 2.0)
schemes.status_note: Fits where the catchment is eroding (silt) or where runoff no longer reaches the waterbody.

schemes.name: Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain (incl. Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari)
schemes.status: Active campaign; Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari 2.0 under way in 2026
schemes.status_note: A convergence campaign rather than a funded scheme: works are funded through VB-G RAM G (earlier MGNREGS), Atal Bhujal, 15th Finance Commission grants and CSR. Rajasthan, for example, was fast-tracking Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari 2.0 works (restoration of lakes and ponds, recharge structures) before the 2026 monsoon.

schemes.name: Atal Bhujal Yojana (Atal Jal)
schemes.status: Verify current period and covered blocks
schemes.status_note: Covers selected water-stressed blocks of seven states, including Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh among the atlas states. Check whether the block is covered.

schemes.name: Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY)
components: new and renovated ponds for inland aquaculture
schemes.status: Active; Rs 2,500 crore in BE 2026-27 (end year not confirmed)
schemes.status_note: Launched in 2020 for five years; it still had a budget allocation of Rs 2,500 crore in 2026-27. In its first six years it supported about 23,285 ha of ponds for inland aquaculture and about 52,000 reservoir cages. Check the current guidelines for the inland pond components.

schemes.name: Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM)
schemes.status_note: SHGs often form the Amrit Sarovar user groups and can take up fishery in village ponds.

schemes.name: Gaal-mukt Dharan, Gaal-yukt Shivar (silt-free dams, silt-rich fields)
schemes.department: Soil and Water Conservation Department, Maharashtra
components: desilting of tanks and small dams
schemes.status_note: Still reported in use in 2025-26 (for example, silt spread on farmland in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar). Separately, in June 2026 Maharashtra revised its policy for desilting large irrigation dams, with silt sold to farmers; that policy is for dams, which this atlas leaves out as reservoirs.

schemes.name: Jalyukt Shivar Abhiyan 2.0
schemes.department: Soil and Water Conservation Department, Maharashtra
components: cement nala bunds and repair of old structures
schemes.status_note: The state government ordered water conservation works under Jalyukt Shivar 2.0 to be done on a war footing ahead of an expected El Niño year.

variables._about: Variables of a waterbody, computed in seft/wb/indicators.py from its yearly water series, its zone of influence, the villages of its home micro-watershed and the MWS drought years; and the fields used to assign its type (seft/wb/build.py). Signals, roles and rules also read the home MWS's variables as mws_<id> (see the watershed variables.json), its system shares as share_<system> and its context classes as ctx_<dimension>. Series are per hydrological year 2017–2024 (July to June).

variables.label: Area
variables.description: Area of the waterbody's mapped extent (area_ored: every pixel that held water in any season of any year), after merging fragments of one waterbody.

variables.label: Catchment ÷ waterbody area
variables.description: Catchment area draining to the waterbody divided by its area. A large ratio means much runoff for its size; a small one, that the catchment may not fill it.

variables.label: Years with water
variables.description: Number of hydrological years 2017–2024 in which any part of the extent held water in kharif.

variables.label: First year with water
variables.description: First hydrological year in which it held water in kharif.

variables.label: New since 2022
variables.description: First wet in 2022 or later and wet in every year since: mostly farm ponds dug recently.

variables.label: Holds water regularly
variables.description: Wet in 3 or more of the 8 years and not new. Most rules are checked only for these.

variables.label: Kharif fill (mean)
variables.description: Mean share of the extent holding water in kharif, over the years with data (k).

questions._about: Community questions for waterbodies. Type questions set the fields that the type rules read (inflow, ownership; types.json) so that the type, and every rule that depends on it, is recomputed. Stress questions carry likelihood ratios (lr) for the rules in rules.json, as in the watershed atlas: the data result sets a prior, each answer multiplies the odds. 'rules' lists the rules a stress question informs; 'applies_to' the types a type question is asked for.

assessment.about: The data result for a rule sets a prior probability that the stress or opportunity is present: higher when it triggered and with higher intensity, pulled toward 50% for lower-confidence rules. Each answer multiplies the odds by its likelihood ratio for that rule. A rule counts as present at positive_at or more.
assessment.partial_rule: Triggered: prior = triggered_min + (triggered_max − triggered_min) × intensity/100. Not triggered: prior = not_triggered + (partial_max − not_triggered) × intensity/100, so partial evidence starts higher. Unknown: 0.4.
assessment.shrink_rule: prior = 0.5 + (base_prior - 0.5) × shrink. A low-confidence rule's data result is held less firmly, so answers move it further.
assessment.severity_rule: A positive rule is severe when the data say severe (intensity at or above the rule's severe_at) and the answers have not lowered its probability, or when an answer marked severe was given and the probability is at least severe_at.
assessment.unknown_rule: A rule with missing data starts just below the positive line (0.4), so it is not counted as present until an answer supports it.

type_questions.text: Who owns this waterbody, and who uses its water?
type_questions.rationale: The data cannot tell a farm pond from a small village pond; the census records ownership (public or private) for every waterbody. A private pond is a farm pond whatever its size; a common pond is a village pond unless it is fed by a stream.
type_questions.origin: New; follows the Water Body Census ownership field

options.label: One farmer or family, on their own land
The village, panchayat or a government department; several families use it

type_questions.text: In the monsoon, where does most of its water come from?
type_questions.rationale: Whether a stream or nala feeds the waterbody decides between an on-stream tank, a headwater pond and a pond filled by runoff from fields; the mapped drainage lines miss small channels and canal feeders.

options.label: A stream or nala flows into it, or it is held by a bund or check dam across one
Rain running off the surrounding fields and slopes; no stream
A canal or a channel from a larger tank fills it

stress_questions.text: Are the channels that bring water into this waterbody working, or are they blocked, broken or cut off?
stress_questions.rationale: Poor filling with an ample catchment usually means the supply channels are silted, broken or cut by roads and fields; a sudden loss can follow a blocked inlet.
stress_questions.origin: New; from the inflow shortfall rule

options.label: They work; water flows in freely
Blocked or cut off by a road, field, wall or another structure

stress_questions.text: Has runoff that used to reach it been diverted upstream, by new fields, roads, check dams or other ponds?
stress_questions.rationale: New structures upstream capture runoff that used to reach older tanks, a common cause of poor filling in intensively treated watersheds.
stress_questions.origin: New; from the inflow shortfall rule

options.label: Some, by a few new structures or fields
A lot; little water reaches it now

stress_questions.text: How much silt has built up since it was last desilted?
stress_questions.rationale: Silt reduces storage both as a falling trend (siltation) and, where it built up before 2017, as poor filling. The census records storage lost to silt for many tanks.
stress_questions.origin: New; from the siltation and inflow rules

options.label: Little; it was desilted in the last few years
Noticeable; it is shallower than before
A lot; much of the bed has filled up

stress_questions.text: Is part of the bed or its edges being farmed or built on?
stress_questions.rationale: Encroachment shrinks the water spread; in the census comparison, encroached waterbodies triggered siltation more often (32% against 21%).
stress_questions.origin: New; from the siltation rule and the census comparison

options.label: A large part, or it has been drained for fields or building

stress_questions.text: Does water leak out through the sluice, outlet or bund?
stress_questions.rationale: Early drying with a full monsoon fill points to leaking sluices and bunds, or to heavy drawal; a breach shows as a sudden loss.

options.label: The sluice or outlet is damaged

stress_questions.text: In a normal year, until when does it hold water?
stress_questions.rationale: How long water lasts decides rabi irrigation, summer water for animals and whether a fish crop (4 to 6 months) is possible; satellite extent can miss shallow water or count wet mud.
stress_questions.origin: New; from the retention, livestock and fishery rules

options.label: Through the summer, or all year

stress_questions.text: In the last drought year, could farmers take water from it to save the kharif crop?
stress_questions.rationale: A tank's main value in semi-arid areas is protective irrigation in dry spells; if it fails exactly then, deepening and catchment work are the remedy.
stress_questions.origin: New; from the drought failure rule

options.label: Yes, enough for most fields that needed it
A little, for a few fields

stress_questions.text: How was its water shared in the last dry season?
stress_questions.rationale: Agreed sharing rules spread the benefit of stored water; their absence is a common reason why water stays unused or goes to a few.
stress_questions.origin: New; from the drought and irrigation rules

options.label: First come, or by those with pumps or influence

stress_questions.text: How many of the fields below or around it are irrigated from it in rabi?
stress_questions.rationale: Water that lasts into rabi with little second-season cropping around it may be unused; the answer separates unused water from cropping limited by other factors.
stress_questions.origin: New; from the irrigation underuse rule

stress_questions.text: Is there a water user association or committee for this waterbody?
stress_questions.rationale: In the census comparison, waterbodies with a water user association triggered irrigation underuse half as often (19% against 40%).

options.label: Yes, and it meets and sets rules

stress_questions.text: Are the field channels and outlets from it working?
stress_questions.rationale: Broken field channels are the most direct reason why stored water does not reach fields.
stress_questions.origin: New; from the irrigation underuse rule

stress_questions.text: Where do animals drink in April to June?
stress_questions.rationale: Where animals are walked far or water is carried, a pond that dries before summer is a real loss.

options.label: Troughs filled from a borewell or tanker
They are taken far, or water is carried

stress_questions.text: Is it used for fishing now, and who holds the rights?
stress_questions.rationale: A waterbody that lasts into rabi where villages fish is a candidate for stocking; unclear rights or pollution make it unsuitable.

options.label: Yes, by a group or cooperative under a lease
Not now, but people want to
No: it dries early, is polluted, or the rights are disputed

stress_questions.text: Does fishing stop early because the water dries up?
stress_questions.rationale: Carp need a culture period of several months; ponds that dry by rabi cut it short.
stress_questions.origin: New; from the fishery constraint rule

stress_questions.text: In the last rabi season, did canal water reach this waterbody when it was needed?
stress_questions.rationale: Tail-end tanks of canal systems get water late or not at all; the answer separates canal supply from local losses.
stress_questions.origin: New; from the canal tail rule

stress_questions.text: Does the river here dry up earlier in summer than it did ten years ago?
stress_questions.rationale: Earlier drying of a river reach follows falling base flow, from pumping near the river and catchment change.

options.label: Much earlier; it is now dry by March or April

stress_questions.text: Is sand mined from this stretch of the river?
stress_questions.rationale: Sand mining lowers the bed and the water table beside it and speeds up drying.

options.label: With machines or on a large scale

notes._about: Rules that write the short introductory note at the top of a waterbody's panel (`waterbody`) and of a group of waterbodies: a micro-watershed, a tehsil or a district (`unit`). For each kind the first `main` rule whose `when` holds gives the opening sentence; every `add` rule whose `when` holds appends its sentence, in order. `when` uses the expression language of the other knowledge files; placeholders in braces are filled from the fields listed in `_fields` (numbers are rounded: whole numbers as they are, others to one decimal). The notes are written by the page from the same data and community answers as the rest of the panel, so they change when answers are applied.

interventions._about: Interventions for water security and ecological restoration, shared by the watershed and waterbody atlases. Supply-side interventions add water (harvest, store, recharge, restore land that lets rain soak in); demand-side interventions reduce or reallocate use (crops, irrigation methods, rules and institutions). Each entry gives where it is built ('where', with the site rules of the CoRE Stack structure-suitability spreadsheet and the ridge-to-valley table of the watershed-development toolkit paper), the landscapes it suits ('landscape', 'archetypes'), a landscape fit test evaluated for each micro-watershed ('suits', 'avoid'), the watershed stresses and waterbody rules it responds to ('addresses', 'addresses_wb', limited to 'wb_types'), schemes that fund it, examples from civil society practice, and sources. Site rules apply to a specific site and need field checks; the fit test only says whether the micro-watershed's landscape is the kind where the intervention usually works.

sides.supply: Adds water or keeps it in the landscape: harvesting, storage, recharge, soil and land restoration.
sides.demand: Reduces or reallocates water use: crops, irrigation methods, rules, institutions and planning.

categories.drainage_line: Drainage-line treatment (across streams, by stream order)
categories.area_treatment: Area treatment on slopes and ridges (off drainage lines)
categories.restoration: Ecological restoration of commons, forest and banks

fit.about: Landscape fit for a micro-watershed (and, in the waterbody atlas, for the waterbody's home micro-watershed): 'suited' when 'suits' holds and 'avoid' does not; 'not suited' when 'avoid' holds; otherwise 'possible'. Expressions read the watershed variables (variables.json), the system shares (share_<archetype>), and the context classes as terrain, aquifer, rainfall, gw_category, canal and cropping. A missing value never makes an intervention suited or unsuited. In the waterbody atlas an intervention is shown for a waterbody only if its type is in 'wb_types' (when given).

levels.suited: The landscape is the kind where this intervention usually works; check the site rules on the ground.
levels.possible: Nothing in the data rules it in or out; decide from site rules and community knowledge.
levels.not suited: The landscape works against it (reason given); consider other interventions first.

community_vars.wl_post_monsoon: Depth to the water level in open wells after the monsoon (m), from the Commons Connect landscape question ls_wl_post; unknown until answered, and then an unknown value changes no verdict.

interventions.site_rules_about: Site rules from the CoRE Stack 'Water structures — suitability rules' workbook, with each value's basis: source (a published manual or paper gives it: the CGWB Manual on Artificial Recharge (2007), the Gujarat IWMP technical manual (2011), the IMSD guidelines (NRSA 1995), NIH (Saha et al. 2018), ICAR-CRIDA's farm pond bulletin (2012), PRADAN's INRM handbook, the Tripura soil and moisture conservation guidelines, the Commons Connect paper), proposed (reasoned from the sources where none gives a number; review before use) or not sourced (no published source found). Site rules are the layers read at the site itself: slope, stream order, catchment area, distance to the nearest drainage line, land use and soil, read as the hydrologic soil group (A–D, from the HYSOGs250m layer the CoRE Stack uses for runoff: A high infiltration, sands; B moderate; C slow; D very slow, clays and shallow soils). The soil type recorded in Commons Connect is kept separately as field data. Rainfall, aquifer, groundwater stage and depth to water belong to the landscape fit ('suits' and 'avoid'); depth to water is asked of the community until a layer exists. Stream order is the CoRE Stack stream order raster: every 30 m pixel carries the Strahler order of the drainage line it drains into, so it is defined off the drainage lines too (plains beside a river carry the river's high order; land beside a gully carries 1). For drainage-line structures it is read on the line, where it equals the line's Strahler order; for area treatments and ponds on farmland it places the land in the ridge-to-valley sequence. Slope in %, catchment in hectares, distance to the nearest drainage line in metres, land use as the CoRE Stack land-use classes. 'site_spec' gives the ridge-to-valley placement.

interventions.name: Loose boulder checks
interventions.what: Small dry-stone barriers across first-order gullies and streams. They slow flash runoff, trap silt and let water soak in; the first treatment of a gully before larger structures downstream.
interventions.where: Drainage line, stream order 1 (up to 3), upper catchment

site_rules.note: Bed slope below 20% (Gujarat).
Read on the drainage-line pixel where the structure goes (distance to drainage line about 0), where the raster value is the Strahler order of that line itself.
Gujarat: drainage lines under 50 ha, each structure with an independent catchment of 1–2 ha; height up to 1 m.

Built across the drainage line, so the site is the line itself: within one 30 m pixel of the mapped line, allowing one more pixel for the offset between the mapped line and the real channel. Gadkari and Kadam weight check dams to within 5–10 m of the channel on a finer network; the Commons Connect paper: water bodies on drainage lines or in their proximity get a reliable surplus runoff.

interventions.landscape: Hilly and undulating land with gullies: forest-fringe, pastoral and upland rainfed micro-watersheds; also above tanks that are silting up.
interventions.avoid_note: Almost no sloping land: few gullies to treat.

interventions.name: Earthen and brushwood gully plugs
interventions.what: Earthen or brushwood plugs in small, steep gullies to stop gully head-cutting and hold silt; usually combined with vegetation on the plug.
interventions.where: Drainage line, stream order 1, steep upper slopes
interventions.site_spec: Earthen gully plugs: across first-order gullies on upper slopes, gully catchments up to 2 ha (medium gullies up to 20 ha), gully bed slopes of about 4–15%; under 2 m deep and 5 m wide

site_rules.note: Gully bed slopes in the Gujarat design table: brushwood 0–5%, earthen 4.5–10.5%, sandbag and masonry 7.5–15%.

CGWB: gully plugs are built across first-order streams. Read on the drainage-line pixel where the structure goes (distance to drainage line about 0), where the raster value is the Strahler order of that line itself.
Small gullies drain up to 2 ha and medium ones 2–20 ha; PRADAN: only gullies under 2 m deep and 5 m wide.

Built across the drainage line, so the site is the line itself: within one 30 m pixel of the mapped line, allowing one more pixel for the offset between the mapped line and the real channel. Gadkari and Kadam weight check dams to within 5–10 m of the channel on a finer network; the Commons Connect paper: water bodies on drainage lines or in their proximity get a reliable surplus runoff.

site_rules.not_accepted: Croplands; Built-up; water in any season

interventions.landscape: Steep, uncultivated slopes under scrub, forest or barren land: forest-fringe and commons-dominated micro-watersheds.
interventions.site_check: Sources: CGWB and Gujarat manuals, PRADAN.

interventions.name: Gabion structures and rock-fill dams
interventions.what: Boulders packed in wire mesh (gabions) or loose rock-fill across second-order streams; flexible, they hold silt and raise local water tables where flows are too strong for loose boulders.
interventions.site_spec: Gabions / rock-fill dams: second-order streams 10–20 m wide with catchments of 30–150 ha; 1–2 m high, keyed into stable banks

site_rules.note: Gabions go across streams 10–20 m wide with 30–150 ha catchments (Gujarat), which in a 30 m drainage network are second- and third-order lines. Read on the drainage-line pixel where the structure goes (distance to drainage line about 0), where the raster value is the Strahler order of that line itself.
Gujarat: gabions for 30–150 ha catchments, 1–2 m high across streams 10–20 m wide.

Built across the drainage line, so the site is the line itself: within one 30 m pixel of the mapped line, allowing one more pixel for the offset between the mapped line and the real channel. Gadkari and Kadam weight check dams to within 5–10 m of the channel on a finer network; the Commons Connect paper: water bodies on drainage lines or in their proximity get a reliable surplus runoff.

site_rules.not_accepted: Trees/forest; Built-up; water in any season

interventions.landscape: Undulating to hilly land with second-order streams in scrub or barren catchments; where stone is available locally.
interventions.avoid_note: Flat: streams too slow for gabions to help.
interventions.site_check: Catchment and stream order from the Gujarat IWMP manual; other rows have no published source.

interventions.name: Check dams, cement nala bunds and anicuts
interventions.what: Masonry or concrete weirs across seasonal streams that store water in the stream bed through the monsoon and recharge the aquifer; downstream wells and fields benefit (the paper estimates the downstream cropping area that a check dam protects).
interventions.where: Drainage line: seasonal streams of order 2 to 3, catchments of about 40 to 500 ha
interventions.site_spec: Check dams, cement nala bunds and anicuts: across a seasonal stream of order 2 to 3 with a catchment of 40 to 500 ha, a gentle bed slope (under about 5%), and a stable, impervious foundation with permeable weathered rock or alluvium upstream so that stored water recharges the aquifer. Larger catchments need a designed spillway and become a percolation tank or small dam

site_rules.note: A gentle bed slope stores more water behind a low wall.

Up to third order (NIH); IMSD allows 1–4; first-order channels take gully plugs and boulder checks. Read on the drainage-line pixel where the structure goes (distance to drainage line about 0), where the raster value is the Strahler order of that line itself.

site_rules.partial: 25–40 ha or 500–1000 ha (masonry check dams with a designed spillway)
site_rules.note: CGWB: 40–100 ha for check dams and cement nala bunds; IMSD and NIH: above 25 ha; Gujarat: masonry check dams normally 500–1000 ha.

Built across the drainage line, so the site is the line itself: within one 30 m pixel of the mapped line, allowing one more pixel for the offset between the mapped line and the real channel. Gadkari and Kadam weight check dams to within 5–10 m of the channel on a finer network; the Commons Connect paper: water bodies on drainage lines or in their proximity get a reliable surplus runoff.

site_rules.accepted: Croplands; single kharif, single non-kharif, double and triple cropping
site_rules.not_accepted: Trees/forest; Built-up; water in any season

site_rules.note: Low to medium permeability under the wall holds the water (NIH: low to medium permeability); some permeability upstream lets it recharge (CGWB).

interventions.landscape: Hard-rock (basalt, granite, gneiss) micro-watersheds with seasonal streams and well-irrigated farms downstream; most useful where the weathered zone can take recharge. Least useful on flat alluvial plains with shallow water tables. As a recharge structure it suits areas with less than about 1000 mm of rain a year (CGWB); in wetter areas it is possible but mainly stores water for irrigation.
interventions.suits: (aquifer == 'hard_rock' or soge_stage >= 70) and f_slopy + f_hill >= 0.15 and nz(rain_norm) < 1000
interventions.avoid: (aquifer == 'alluvium' and terrain == 'plain' and nz(soge_stage) < 70 and rain_norm >= 1000) or (known(wl_post_monsoon) and wl_post_monsoon < 3)
interventions.avoid_note: Flat, humid alluvial plain with a shallow, safe water table: little room for extra recharge and a risk of waterlogging.
interventions.caution: Upstream structures cut inflow to tanks and check dams downstream (Wable et al. 2022); plan at micro-watershed scale and keep part of the runoff flowing. Desilt regularly.
practice: Saurashtra (Gujarat): check-dam and well-recharge movement of the 1990s, led by farmers and diamond merchants
Ralegan Siddhi and Hiware Bazar (Ahmednagar, Maharashtra): cement nala bunds and check dams with village rules on water use
Utthan, Bhavnagar (Gujarat): check dams in the paper's Morchand village plan
interventions.site_check: Sources: CGWB, IMSD, NIH (Saha et al. 2018), Gujarat IWMP manual. Rainfall is part of the landscape fit, not the site rules. Soil as the hydrologic soil group (HYSOGs250m).

interventions.name: Percolation tanks
interventions.what: Shallow tanks on second- and third-order streams sited over permeable strata so that stored water percolates to wells downstream within a few months, rather than being used directly.
interventions.where: Drainage line, stream order 2–3, gentle slopes

site_rules.note: Land slope at the tank site; IMSD allows percolation ponds up to 10%.
Read on the drainage-line pixel where the structure goes (distance to drainage line about 0), where the raster value is the Strahler order of that line itself.
CGWB: 2.5–4 km² for small and 5–8 km² for large tanks; IMSD sites percolation ponds from 25 ha.
On a second- or third-order stream (CGWB); the water spread extends beside the line.

site_rules.accepted: Croplands; single kharif, single non-kharif, double and triple cropping
site_rules.not_accepted: Trees/forest; Built-up; water in any season

site_rules.note: The tank bed must let stored water through to the aquifer (CGWB; IMSD: permeable soils): groups A and B; group D clays seal the bed.

interventions.landscape: Hard-rock areas with a weathered or fractured zone and falling water levels, in semi-arid and dry sub-humid climates; gently sloping cropland with wells downstream. Not where the water level after the monsoon is within 3 m of the ground: there is no room in the aquifer and the land waterlogs (CGWB; asked of the community, since the CoRE Stack has no depth-to-water layer yet).
interventions.suits: aquifer == 'hard_rock' and nz(soge_stage) >= 70 and rainfall in ['semi_arid', 'dry_subhumid'] and not (known(wl_post_monsoon) and wl_post_monsoon < 3)
interventions.avoid_note: Saline aquifer: recharge water mixes with saline groundwater.
interventions.caution: Silt seals the bed within a few years; desilt and treat the catchment. Check the strata: over massive rock with no weathered zone, water evaporates instead of recharging.
interventions.site_spec: Percolation tanks: on second- or third-order streams with catchments of about 2.5–8 km² (250–800 ha), land slope 3–5%, permeable weathered or fractured rock or alluvium beneath the tank, and a water table deeper than 3 m after the monsoon; the tank should normally empty by February (CGWB)
interventions.site_check: Sources: CGWB and Gujarat IWMP manuals, which agree, and IMSD. Depth to water is part of the landscape fit, asked of the community. Soil as the hydrologic soil group (HYSOGs250m).

interventions.name: Sub-surface dykes (underground bandharas)
interventions.what: An impermeable wall dug across a stream bed down to bedrock, holding groundwater in the sand and gravel upstream; it keeps wells beside the stream wet into summer without surface evaporation.
interventions.where: Stream or river beds with sandy fill over shallow bedrock
interventions.landscape: Seasonal rivers and wide nalas with sandy beds in hard-rock or coastal areas; drinking-water wells near the stream.
interventions.avoid_note: No river or upstream inflow through the micro-watershed.

interventions.name: Diversion-based irrigation
interventions.what: Small weirs that divert part of a perennial or long-flowing stream into gravity channels to fields, without pumps or large storage; a traditional system in hill areas.
interventions.where: Hill streams that flow beyond the monsoon
interventions.landscape: Hilly, sub-humid and humid tribal areas with streams that flow into rabi: forest-fringe and rainfed-rice micro-watersheds (for example Koraput, Godda).
interventions.suits: terrain == 'hilly' and rainfall in ['dry_subhumid', 'humid'] and (river_present >= 1 or n_upstream >= 1)
interventions.avoid_note: Streams do not flow long enough after the monsoon.
practice: Hill streams in Odisha and Jharkhand: diversion-based irrigation promoted by NGOs such as PRADAN and by state minor-irrigation programmes

interventions.name: Continuous contour trenches (CCT)
interventions.what: Trenches dug along the contour on uncultivated slopes; they stop sheet runoff, hold soil and moisture for grass and saplings, and recharge the aquifer below.
interventions.where: Ridges and upper slopes, non-cultivated land
interventions.site_spec: Ridges and steep slopes of 10–25%, non-cultivated land

site_rules.note: Gujarat: not below 10% (use contour bunds) or above 25%; Tripura: 10–30%; PRADAN: trenches above 8%.

Raster value of the land itself: the Strahler order of the drainage line its runoff reaches. Low values (1–3) are upper catchment land draining to gullies and small nalas, where area treatment belongs; the slope rule does most of the work.

Area treatment belongs on the slopes between drainage lines and intercepts overland flow; a drainage line within one pixel is treated with gully plugs and checks instead (ridge-to-valley sequence, PRADAN). Proposed: no published distance found.

interventions.landscape: Ridges and upper slopes under scrub, open forest or barren commons; the first step of ridge-to-valley treatment in hard-rock watersheds.
interventions.avoid_note: Almost no uncultivated land to trench.
interventions.caution: On slopes over 25% or in shallow soils use staggered trenches; avoid trenching dense natural forest.
practice: Watershed Organisation Trust (WOTR), Ahmednagar: ridge-to-valley treatment starting with CCT on hill slopes
interventions.site_check: Sources: Gujarat IWMP manual, Tripura guidelines, IMSD, PRADAN.

interventions.site_spec: Ridges and steep slopes of 10–25% (paper, Table 1)

interventions.name: Trench-cum-bund networks (TCB)
interventions.what: Lines of trenches with the dug soil formed into a bund below, on gentle slopes and fallows; they harvest sheet runoff for recharge. The paper's Mala Khera (Bhilwara) plan projects that a TCB network protects about 13 ha of downstream crops and one well.

interventions.name: Contour bunds
interventions.what: Earthen bunds along the contour on sloping farmland; they hold runoff on the field so that it soaks in, and keep soil and moisture on the field.

interventions.name: Graded bunds
interventions.what: Earthen bunds laid with a slight grade along the slope, so that excess runoff drains slowly to a grassed waterway or safe outlet instead of standing on the field; they keep soil on the field in wetter areas and on clays.

site_rules.note: Raster value of the land itself: the Strahler order of the drainage line its runoff reaches. Low values (1–3) are upper catchment land draining to gullies and small nalas, where area treatment belongs; the slope rule does most of the work.

Area treatment belongs on the slopes between drainage lines and intercepts overland flow; a drainage line within one pixel is treated with gully plugs and checks instead (ridge-to-valley sequence, PRADAN). Proposed: no published distance found.

site_rules.accepted: Single kharif, single non-kharif, double, triple cropping; croplands; barren lands; shrub/scrub; trees/forest

site_rules.note: Graded bunds lead excess water away to a waterway, so they also suit slowly permeable group D soils, where contour bunds would waterlog (CGWB).

interventions.landscape: Rainfed cropland on slopes where rainfall is normally 800 mm or more, and on slowly permeable clays, where contour bunds would waterlog the field (CGWB).
interventions.suits: nz(share_rainfed_dryland) + nz(share_rainfed_rice_subhumid) >= 0.2 and f_slopy >= 0.1 and rain_norm >= 800
interventions.site_check: Sources: Gujarat IWMP manual, CGWB; soil as the hydrologic soil group (HYSOGs250m).

interventions.name: Farm (field) bunds
interventions.what: Low earthen bunds around field boundaries on flat cropland, including paddy bunds, that hold rainwater and silt on the field and mark the plot; they raise soil moisture and, in rice, keep standing water in the field.
interventions.where: On farm, flat land below 3% slope
interventions.site_spec: Field boundaries on flat cropland below 3% slope (PRADAN: field bunding below 3%)

site_rules.note: PRADAN: field bunding below 3%; on gentler slopes above that, contour or graded bunds.

Area treatment belongs on the slopes between drainage lines and intercepts overland flow; a drainage line within one pixel is treated with gully plugs and checks instead (ridge-to-valley sequence, PRADAN). Proposed: no published distance found.

site_rules.accepted: Single kharif, single non-kharif, double, triple cropping
site_rules.not_accepted: Trees/forest; Built-up; water in any season

interventions.landscape: Flat rainfed cropland, especially rainfed rice in sub-humid areas, where neither contour nor graded bunds apply.
interventions.site_check: Slope from PRADAN; land use from the CoRE Stack rules workbook; distance to drainage line proposed.

interventions.name: Stone bunding and stone terraces
interventions.what: Bunds of field stones around waste and fallow land and stony fields; they hold soil and let water through, and bring degraded land back into use.
interventions.where: Broad slopes (6–10%) off farm, around waste and fallow land
interventions.site_spec: Broad slopes 6–10% off farm: stone bunding around waste and fallow lands (paper, Table 1)

site_rules.note: Raster value of the land itself: the Strahler order of the drainage line its runoff reaches. Low values (1–3) are upper catchment land draining to gullies and small nalas, where area treatment belongs; the slope rule does most of the work.

Area treatment belongs on the slopes between drainage lines and intercepts overland flow; a drainage line within one pixel is treated with gully plugs and checks instead (ridge-to-valley sequence, PRADAN). Proposed: no published distance found.
